title: MedFusion-gP-AKI: development and multicenter validation of a machine learning fusion model for early prediction of KDIGO stage 3 acute kidney injury in critically ill traumatic cervicothoracic spinal cord injury patients

paragraphs.en: Critically ill traumatic cervicothoracic spinal cord injury (TCTSCI) patients often develop neurogenic shock due to abrupt sympathetic dysfunction, leading to systemic vasodilation, arterial hypoperfusion, and inadequate multiorgan perfusion, which rapidly reduces renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in the early phase [1]. Simultaneously, the systemic inflammatory response extends beyond the injured spinal cord to distant organs such as the kidneys, characterized by early immune cell infiltration and sustained proinflammatory cytokine expression, further aggravating kidney injury under impaired microcirculation [2]. This combined impact of hemodynamic collapse and immune-mediated inflammation contributes to the high incidence of acute kidney injury (AKI), a common and critical complication in TCTSCI [3]. Galeiras et al. [4] reported that over half of traumatic spinal cord injury (TSCI) patients develop AKI early after injury, with even higher rates in critically ill cases, while KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) stage 3 AKI has been independently linked to poor short-term outcomes and, as further reported by Yu et al. [5] serves as a predictor of failure to discontinue mechanical ventilation in patients with high cervical injury, highlighting the pivotal role of early kidney dysfunction in clinical management and short-term prognosis in critically ill TCTSCI patients.

Furthermore, in critically ill TCTSCI patients, AKI may pose long-term health risks beyond the acute phase, as residual kidney damage, even after a partial recovery, easily tends to progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD), which, in the context of TCTSCI, further disrupts blood pressure regulation and markedly increases cardiovascular risk [6]. Given that cardiovascular complications are the leading cause of late mortality in chronic TCTSCI, the prevention of secondary organ dysfunction, particularly kidney impairment, is considered as important as promoting neurological recovery in improving long-term survival and quality of life [7].

Accordingly, early identification of high-risk KDIGO stage 3 AKI individuals in critically ill TCTSCI patients is essential to preserve the intervention window for timely intervention measures such as hemodynamic optimization and avoidance of nephrotoxic agents, yet no predictive model tailored to this population using routine admission data is currently available [8]. To address this gap, this study develops the first TCTSCI-specific, causality-guided, generative-augmented ensemble AI ecosystem (see Novelty Overview Box for detailed innovations) for early KDIGO stage 3 AKI prediction by leveraging machine learning on clinical information collected within the first 24 h of admission, encompassing laboratory results, vital signs, and baseline characteristics, with model training and internal validation performed on the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) and electronic Intensive Care Unit Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) databases and external validation conducted across four tertiary hospitals in China to ensure generalizability. Built upon this integrative multicenter framework, the tool is designed to enable early risk stratification, guide timely intervention, improve acute-phase management, reduce AKI-related mortality, and help prevent the long-term progression of chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular complications.

This study developed machine learning models to predict the short-term (7-day) risk of AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients using data from MIMIC-IV v3.1 [9] and eICU-CRD v2.0 [10], two publicly available databases curated by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, with institutional review board approval and informed consent waiver (Certification No. 57264471). To evaluate the generalizability of the model across different healthcare systems, external validation was performed using data from critically ill TCTSCI patients admitted between January 2021 and January 2025 across four tertiary hospitals in China, with ethics approval obtained from each participating center (The First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University: K202404-45; People’s Hospital of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region: KY2024052264; Chongqing University Three Gorges Hospital: SXYYWD2022-058; Jingzhou First People’s Hospital: YJ202376). Figure 1 outlines the complete analytic workflow, encompassing data preprocessing, model construction, and evaluation steps.

Critically ill TCTSCI patients were identified from MIMIC-IV v3.1 and eICU-CRD v2.0 using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes, with individuals under 18 years of age or with substantial missing data excluded, and only the first ICU admission was retained for those with multiple stays to avoid duplication. Structured data were extracted using Navicat Premium 15 (PremiumSoft CyberTech Ltd., Hong Kong, China), and external validation data were manually collected from electronic medical records of four tertiary hospitals. To ensure early clinical applicability, all model features were restricted to variables recorded within 24 h of ICU admission. Collected data included 7-day AKI occurrence and relevance KDIGO stage, 60-day survival status, and clinical variables, including demographic characteristics (e.g., age), clinical scores (e.g., Charlson Comorbidity Index), vital signs (e.g., heart rate), TSCI-Level, therapeutic interventions [e.g., Vasopressor-Use (VP-Use)], and laboratory tests (e.g., electrolytes), all used for model development and evaluation.

sections.title: Outcome stratification according to KDIGO AKI stage

paragraphs.en: To evaluate prognostic differences across KDIGO AKI stages in critically ill TCTSCI patients and provide data-driven outcome definition for subsequent machine learning, this study categorized patients into four groups based on KDIGO 2012 criteria [11], including no AKI, stage 1, stage 2, and stage 3, and performed a 60-day survival analysis [12] using admission data from MIMIC-IV and eICU. Survival time was defined as the number of days from first ICU admission to death, and 60-day survival status was determined from recorded death dates. Kaplan–Meier curves and log-rank tests were applied to compare survival across groups and to identify early high-risk subpopulations. Patients with KDIGO stage 3 AKI exhibited markedly reduced 60-day survival compared with those in lower AKI stages, underscoring the prognostic importance of stage 3 AKI as a clinically meaningful endpoint for early risk prediction (as detailed in the Results section 3.1).

After extracting clinical data of critically ill TCTSCI patients from MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD, variables with over 30% missingness were removed, and the remaining gaps were imputed using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) [13], which captured nonlinear data patterns to improve structural consistency and data completeness. External validation datasets, manually collected from four hospitals, contained no missing values.

Univariate analysis was first conducted to compare patients with KDIGO stage 3 AKI and those without, identifying candidate predictors that showed significant differences in demographics, vital signs, laboratory values, TSCI characteristics, and therapeutic interventions, thereby reducing the risk of false positives. To further extract stable and causally relevant features from the high-dimensional dataset, a structured selection framework was implemented using three independent methods. Autoencoder with Causal Attention Embedding (ACAE) captured latent dependency structures through causal attention to derive compressed representations aligned with underlying causal relationships [14]. Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB) applies the information bottleneck principle to retain target-relevant features while discarding redundant signals [15]. Non-combinatorial Optimization via Trace Exponential and Augmented lagRangian for Structure learning (NOTEARS) inferred a directed acyclic graph under continuous constraints to identify direct-effect variables with independent predictive value [16]. The intersection of features selected by all three approaches was used to construct the final feature set, optimizing both interpretability and non-redundancy. Pearson correlation heatmaps were used to evaluate linear associations, followed by the calculation of variance inflation factors (VIF) to further eliminate variables with multicollinearity risk, thereby enhancing model robustness and generalizability.

The study found that 14.0% of critically ill TCTSCI patients developed KDIGO stage 3 AKI within seven days, indicating class imbalance and challenges in minority class recognition. To avoid the risk of overfitting and distribution distortion associated with conventional SMOTE in high-dimensional continuous data, a Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique enhanced by Generative Adversarial Network (SMOTified-GAN) approach was adopted [17]. Unlike traditional SMOTE, which interpolates between existing samples, SMOTified-GAN learns the global latent distribution of the minority class to generate statistically independent, high-fidelity synthetic data [18]. In line with recent studies supporting full-dataset SMOTified-GAN augmentation before internal splitting, this study adopted this approach to maximize representational diversity and prevent sampling bias between training and validation cohorts while capturing nonlinear structure, preserving feature integrity, stabilizing class balance, and enabling robust, well-calibrated model development [19–21].

Statistical analyses were conducted in R 4.3.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), with categorical variables summarized as counts and percentages, and continuous variables reported as medians with interquartile ranges. For group comparisons, the chi-squared test was used when all expected frequencies were at least five, whereas Fisher’s exact test was applied when this assumption was violated. Continuous variables were first assessed for normality, with those meeting the assumption analyzed using the independent-samples t-test, and those violating the assumption evaluated using the Mann-Whitney U test. All p-values were two-sided, and statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05.

Machine learning modeling and interpretability analyses were conducted in Python 3.8.10 (Python Software Foundation, Delaware, USA), following the TRIPOD-AI and PROBAST-AI guidelines to ensure comprehensive adherence to best practices in the development, validation, transparent reporting, and risk-of-bias assessment of artificial intelligence–based predictive models [22,23]. Modeling was performed using both the original and SMOTified-GAN balanced datasets, each randomly partitioned into training and internal validation sets at a 7:3 ratio. A total of fifteen individual models were evaluated, including eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Tabular Network (TabNet), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Self-Attention and Intersample Attention Transformer (SAINT), Neural Oblivious Decision Ensemble (NODE), Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), Feature Tokenizer Transformer (FT-Transformer), Deep Kernel Learning (DKL), Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Each model underwent hyperparameter optimization via five-fold cross-validation. Performance was comprehensively assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves with corresponding area under the curve (AUC), precision–recall (PR) curves with average precision (AP), calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and gain curves, with additional evaluation at a classification threshold of 0.5 using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1 score.

The ensemble model, MedFusion-GP-AKI, was developed by integrating the core architectures and classification strategies of the best-performing individual models and was trained and evaluated on both pre-SMOTE and SMOTified-GAN balanced training and validation sets, ensuring consistency in data partitioning and performance comparability, while its robustness and cross-institutional generalizability were validated using external clinical data from four tertiary hospitals (The First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University; People’s Hospital of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region; Chongqing University Three Gorges Hospital; Jingzhou First People’s Hospital). Model interpretability was assessed using Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis, which generated both global feature attributions rankings and individual-level explanatory visualizations. Intended for real-time clinical deployment, the final model will support the development of an interactive online calculator to assist with early prediction and risk stratification of KDIGO stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients.

sections.title: Survival outcomes across KDIGO AKI stages

paragraphs.en: Based on predefined criteria, 996 critically ill TCTSCI patients were included from the MIMIC-IV 3.1 and eICU 2.0 databases and categorized into four subgroups according to KDIGO staging, including no AKI (n = 406), stage 1 (n = 152), stage 2 (n = 298), and stage 3 (n = 140). Kaplan–Meier curves demonstrated a significant stepwise decline in 60-day survival with increasing AKI severity (log-rank p < 0.001; Figure 2). Among critically ill TCTSCI patients, those with KDIGO stage 3 AKI had the poorest outcomes, with a 60-day mortality of 49.3% and a median survival of 20 days [IQR 10–37], whereas stages 0–2 showed mortality rates of 4.7%, 10.5%, and 16.1%, each exceeding 60 days of median survival. The persistence of survival differences even between stages 1 and 2 indicates that AKI severity correlates closely with long-term prognosis. Collectively, these findings establish KDIGO stage 3 AKI as a clinically meaningful indicator of critical illness progression and provide the rationale for defining its occurrence within 7 days after ICU admission as the primary prediction endpoint, with mortality analyses serving to contextualize outcome severity.

To explore early clinical characteristics linked to short-term development of KDIGO stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients, univariate comparisons were conducted using a binary grouping based on whether stage 3 AKI occurred within the first seven days of admission. Before statistical analysis, missing clinical variables were imputed using the GAN-based approach, whose results were further compared with conventional imputation methods to ensure data reliability (see Supplementary Material 1). Among 996 patients, those who developed KDIGO stage 3 AKI (n = 140) showed significant differences from non-stage 3 patients (n = 856) across multiple domains (Table 1). Patients who progressed to stage 3 AKI were older and had lower body weight (both p < 0.001), with significantly higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores (both p < 0.001), and lower Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores (p < 0.001), indicating greater chronic disease burden and more severe baseline organ dysfunction. Hemodynamic parameters in the stage 3 AKI group showed reduced heart rate (HR), respiratory rate (RR), systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and mean arterial pressure (MAP), suggesting increased circulatory instability. Laboratory indicators in the stage 3 AKI group revealed elevated glucose, lactate, and serum potassium levels (all p < 0.001), along with higher white blood cell counts (p = 0.015), while serum sodium and bicarbonate (HCO3-) concentrations were significantly lower (both p < 0.001), indicating metabolic disturbance and systemic hypoperfusion. Moreover, patients who developed stage 3 AKI exhibited lower body temperature (Temp), less frequent VP-Use (both p < 0.001), and a higher prevalence of cervical cord injuries (TSCI-Level) (p < 0.001).

Among the variables identified through univariate analysis, SBP, DBP, and MAP exhibited substantial collinearity, and MAP was retained due to clinical experience and relevance. To further refine the candidate set, three independent algorithms were employed, with the VIB method identifying 15 variables characterized by high information retention as shown in Figure 3a, the NOTEARS algorithm selecting 13 features exhibiting direct causal relevance as depicted in Figure 3b, and the ACAE approach yielding 14 predictors based on counterfactual perturbation analysis as illustrated in Figure 3c. By integrating the intersection of variables derived from the three selection approaches, a final subset of 11 key predictors was obtained, each demonstrating consistent relevance across information compression capacity, causal structural dependencies, and counterfactual perturbation analysis. This variable set encompassed multiple dimensions of pathophysiological status associated with high risk for stage 3 AKI in TCTSCI patients, including CCI, GCS, HR, MAP, Temp, lactate, WBC, VP-Use, and TSCI-Level (Figure 3d). Correlation heatmaps (Figure 3e) and VIF analyses (Figure 3f) confirmed low multicollinearity among these variables (all VIF < 5), supporting their use as robust, independent inputs for subsequent model development and generalization evaluation.

All models underwent hyperparameter tuning via five-fold cross-validated optimization on both the original and SMOTified-GAN training cohorts, with the tuned parameters summarized in Supplementary Table 1. On the original, highly imbalanced dataset, all models showed limited discrimination, fragile calibration, and minimal net clinical benefit, with detailed results provided in Supplementary Material 2. Using SMOTified-GAN, the number of critically ill TCTSCI patients with KGIGO stage 3 AKI increased from 140 to 919, balanced against 856 without stage 3 AKI. Across both the training (Figure 4a–4f) and internal validation (Figure 5a–5f) sets, the fifteen candidate models exhibited heterogeneous performance in discrimination (Figure 4a/5a), precision-recall metrics (Figure 4b/5b), net clinical benefit (Figure 4c/5c), calibration (Figure 4d/5d), gain-based ranking (Figure 4e/5e), and radar-based composite evaluation (Figure 4f/5f). TabNet demonstrated relatively strong performance with AUCs of 0.879 and 0.853 and APs of 0.878 and 0.867 across training and internal validation, ranking highly on ROC and PR curves while maintaining close alignment between predicted and observed risks in calibration, delivering net clinical benefit across most threshold intervals, and exhibiting a sharply rising gain curve that indicated robust capacity to identify true positives within the top 20% high-risk population. NODE and DKL yielded comparably stable results across both training and internal validation cohorts, with NODE achieving AUCs of 0.867 and 0.873 and APs of 0.872 and 0.873, and DKL reaching AUCs of 0.879 and 0.871 with APs of 0.859 and 0.879, all reflecting reliable discrimination, calibration consistency, and stratification capacity across both cohorts. SAINT maintained balanced AUC and AP values of 0.862 and 0.865 and 0.848 and 0.863, respectively, with calibration deviations confined to the mid-probability range and moderate gain performance. RF and FT-Transformer showed high scores during training but experienced marked degradation in validation, with AUCs declining to 0.812 and 0.811 and APs to 0.813 and 0.802, respectively, suggesting potential overfitting as corroborated by flatter gain slopes and radar plots indicating suboptimal specificity and precision. Classical algorithms, including logistic regression, LightGBM, SVM, GBM, CatBoost, and MLP, generally produced AUC and AP values ranging from 0.7 to 0.8, yet their net benefit often approximated the treat-none baseline under medium to high thresholds, with shallow gain curves and no evident advantage in accuracy, sensitivity, or F1 score. KNN displayed considerable performance fluctuation, with AUCs of 0.854 and 0.693 and APs of 0.817 and 0.711, accompanied by unstable calibration and inconsistent gain. XGBoost ranked consistently lowest across nearly all evaluation metrics, including AUCs of 0.763 and 0.710 and APs of 0.742 and 0.716, and exhibited poor discrimination, limited clinical utility, and compact radar plot patterns.

Although TabNet, SAINT, NODE, and DKL performed relatively well in discrimination and generalizability, each exhibited limitations in calibration, risk ranking, and high-threshold clinical benefit. To overcome these shortcomings, research developed the ensemble MedFusion-GP-AKI, which integrates these complementary learners at the representation level rather than through conventional stacking. This unified fusion framework enables shared feature learning and uncertainty-aware prediction, thereby improving robustness and reliability across heterogeneous critically ill TCTSCI populations, with detailed architectural information provided in Supplementary Material 3.

To mitigate potential overestimation of performance from synthetic oversampling, the MedFusion-GP-AKI model was evaluated across pre- and post-SMOTE training and internal validation cohorts, enabling a direct assessment of whether performance gains represented genuine improvement in minority-class learning rather than artifacts of oversampling or data leakage. To further examine external validity and cross-institutional robustness, an independent external cohort of 188 critically ill TCTSCI patients was assembled between January 2021 and January 2025 from four tertiary medical centers, including 74 from the First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University, 61 from the People’s Hospital of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, 28 from Chongqing University Three Gorges Hospital, and 25 from Jingzhou First People’s Hospital, among whom 67 developed KDIGO stage 3 AKI and 121 did not, with baseline characteristics summarized in Supplementary Table 2.

In the pre-SMOTE training cohort, MedFusion-GP-AKI achieved an AUC of 0.938 and an AP of 0.841, indicating strong discrimination even before class rebalancing, with the pre-SMOTE internal validation set showing comparable performance (AUC = 0.900; AP = 0.838). Following SMOTE augmentation, both the training (AUC = 0.969; AP = 0.992) and internal validation (AUC = 0.945; AP = 0.927) sets demonstrated modest improvement in sensitivity within high-recall regions, consistent with enhanced minority-class representation rather than overfitting. Importantly, the external cohort maintained robust discriminative capacity (AUC = 0.921; AP = 0.878), confirming that model performance generalized well across independent institutions (Figure 6a and 6b).

DCA (Figure 6c) demonstrated that MedFusion-GP-AKI consistently delivered clinically meaningful net benefit across all datasets. In the pre-SMOTE training and internal validation sets, the model achieved clear separation from both the treat-all and treat-none strategies within the clinically relevant probability range, indicating sound risk calibration and practical applicability even before synthetic balancing. Following SMOTE augmentation, both the training and internal test curves exhibited a modest upward shift in net benefit, reflecting improved detection of high-risk cases without loss of specificity. Notably, the external validation cohort produced a nearly parallel curve to the post-SMOTE internal validation set, confirming that the model’s decision-level utility generalized effectively across independent institutional data. Calibration assessment (Figure 6d) demonstrated that the mild underestimation observed in the pre-SMOTE models was alleviated after class balancing, with Brier scores decreasing from 0.096 (pre-SMOTE train) and 0.101 (pre-SMOTE internal validation) to 0.033 (SMOTE train) and 0.063 (SMOTE internal validation), while the external cohort exhibited a score of 0.149, indicating acceptable probability calibration across heterogeneous clinical settings. Consistently, calibration-in-the-large (CITL) improved from −1.69 (pre-SMOTE train) and −1.91 (pre-SMOTE internal validation) to −0.02 (SMOTE train) and −0.10 (SMOTE internal validation), with −0.33 in the external validation, reflecting effective correction of underestimation bias following SMOTE balancing. Detailed calibration statistics are provided in Supplementary Table 3.

The cumulative-gain analysis (Figure 6e) further confirmed a consistent and transferable risk-ranking capability across all datasets, as the model effectively prioritized true AKI cases within the top-risk strata in both pre-SMOTE and post-SMOTE conditions. The pre-SMOTE curves remained well above the random baseline, while the post-SMOTE cohorts exhibited slightly steeper cumulative-gain curves in the training and internal validation sets, reflecting enhanced recall for high-risk patients and confirming that discrimination was not merely a consequence of oversampling. The external cohort also showing a closely aligned pattern underscored the model’s robustness and stability across heterogeneous clinical populations. The radar-plot summary (Figure 6f) shows that model performance before oversampling was not uniformly balanced, with the pre-SMOTE test cohort lagging in precision and F1 and showing slightly lower specificity and sensitivity than the other datasets. After SMOTE, both the training and internal validation cohorts displayed broader radar profiles, achieving the largest gains in sensitivity and F1 while maintaining comparable specificity and accuracy. The external cohort remains close to the post-SMOTE internal curves, with a small drop in sensitivity and F1 but accuracy and specificity comparable to internal results, indicating robustness across heterogeneous populations.

Together, these findings demonstrate that MedFusion-GP-AKI maintains robust discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility across pre- and post-SMOTE datasets and multi-institutional validation, confirming its generalizability and excluding the likelihood of data leakage or inflated performance.

In the interpretability analysis of MedFusion-GP-AKI, the SHAP framework was used to quantify each variable’s marginal contribution to predicting KDIGO stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients. Global feature attributions derived from SHAP explainability (Figure 7a) identified lactate, MAP, and serum potassium as dominant contributors aligned with physiologic pathways involving renal perfusion, acid–base imbalance, hemodynamic, and electrolyte disturbance, while temperature, TSCI level, and GCS further reflected integrated metabolic and neurologic disruptions captured by the model. The summary plot (Figure 7b) revealed distinct directional effects, where higher lactate, lower temperature, and lower GCS pushed predictions toward high risk, while higher MAP, lower serum potassium, and lower-segmental spinal cord injuries were associated with low-risk outputs. At the individual level, predictions for KDIGO stage 3 AKI cases (Figure 7c) were driven by positive contributions from lactate (+0.30), serum potassium (+0.04), and MAP (+0.07), raising outputs above the baseline (E[f(x)]≈0.48). Conversely, non-AKI predictions (Figure 7d) were suppressed by low serum potassium (–0.18), caudal injury level (–0.12), and low heart rate (–0.10), shifting outputs away from high-risk zones.

sections.title: TRIPOD-AI and PROBAST-AI reporting evaluation of MedFusion-GP-AKI

paragraphs.en: The MedFusion-GP-AKI model was appraised using the TRIPOD-AI and PROBAST-AI frameworks, which jointly demonstrated transparent reporting and a low overall risk of methodological bias. The TRIPOD-AI review confirmed clear specification of data sources and eligibility criteria, explicit definitions of predictors and outcomes, and reproducible descriptions of model development and validation, all conforming to AI-focused reporting standards. The PROBAST-AI evaluation indicated a consistently low risk of bias, supported by harmonized multi-center inclusion, standardized predictor preprocessing, and rigorous analytical procedures for imputation, class balancing, and calibration. Overall, owing to the exclusive use of routinely collected clinical variables and standardized outcomes, the model was deemed highly applicable for early ICU risk prediction. Detailed evaluation results are provided in Supplementary Material 3 (TRIPOD-AI) and Supplementary Material 4 (PROBAST-AI).

A web-based calculator (https://aki-predict.streamlit.app/) was developed based on the MedFusion-GP-AKI model to demonstrate its potential for clinical integration. The calculator provides an interactive interface through which clinicians can enter routinely collected ICU data from the first 24 h after admission and immediately obtain an individualized probability of developing KDIGO stage 3 AKI, along with a visual display of key contributing predictors. Figure 8 illustrates the overall interface design and operational workflow, highlighting how the tool integrates seamlessly into early ICU risk assessment.

To demonstrate how an ICU physician could apply the MedFusion-GP-AKI calculator at the bedside, a prospective observational case was documented in a critically ill TCTSCI patient. Within 24 h of ICU admission, the attending physician entered the patient’s initial clinical parameters into the web interface as follows: spinal cord injury level: low cervical; vasopressor administration: None; GCS: 7; CCI: 5; HR: 64 beats/min; MAP: 78 mmHg; Temperature: 36 °C; WBC: 12 × 109/L; bicarbonate: 13.01 mmol/L; potassium: 3.70 mmol/L; lactate: 3.40 mmol/L. The calculator generated a predicted probability of 78.3% for developing KDIGO stage 3 AKI within seven days. During routine ICU monitoring, the patient subsequently met the KDIGO criteria for stage 3 AKI on day 5, confirming the model’s accurate early risk estimation in a real-world clinical context. This observation, conducted without any interventional influence on clinical management, exemplifies how the calculator can be incorporated into real-time ICU workflows to provide early, non-intrusive risk assessment and to enhance physicians’ situational awareness for timely recognition of patients at elevated renal risk.

Notably, all prediction fields in the calculator must be completed to ensure valid computation. Because the required variables correspond to standard ICU measurements, missing data at prediction time are rare. If any field is incomplete, the interface prompts the user to confirm or correct the entry before calculation.

This study introduces MedFusion-GP-AKI, a deep learning model designed to predict short-term KDIGO stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients. Using clinical data from the first 24 h of ICU admission, the model incorporates predictors spanning ICU scoring systems (GCS, CCI), routine assessments (HR, MAP, Temp, WBC, HCO3-, K+, Lac), therapeutic interventions (VP-Use), and TSCI-specific variables (TSCI-Level), which were selected through a causality-guided pipeline integrating VIB, NOTEARS, and ACAE. Built upon a unified multimodal architecture that combines complementary learning modules to capture nonlinear clinical interactions and quantify predictive uncertainty, MedFusion-GP-AKI achieved strong discrimination and generalizability across both internal and multi-center external cohorts, supporting early risk stratification and management of KDIGO stage 3 AKI following TCTSCI.

In the MedFusion-GP-AKI model, lactate emerged as a dominant predictor of short-term stage 3 AKI risk among TCTSCI patients, reflecting its high sensitivity to circulatory compromise and its established role as a biomarker of tissue hypoperfusion in critical illness [24]. Previous studies have shown that lactate levels rise rapidly following spinal cord injury [25], with Falconer et al. reporting increases to two to five times baseline within 20 to 60 min post-injury, preceding alterations in other metabolic indicators [26]. Yousefifard et al. further demonstrated a strong association between elevated lactate and short-term adverse outcomes in TSCI, supporting its value in early prognostication [27]. The pathophysiological basis of hyperlactatemia in TCTSCI likely involves post-traumatic hemorrhage and neurogenic cardiopulmonary dysfunction, both of which reduce systemic perfusion and exacerbate renal susceptibility [28,29]. Notably, elevated lactate levels have been consistently associated with increased AKI risk in critical illness, with Nasu et al. identifying concentrations ≥2.5 mmol/L as significantly predictive of severe AKI and poor outcomes [30], and Wang et al. further demonstrated that early lactate elevation in traumatic brain injury patients serves as a reliable marker for AKI development [31]. Consistent with these findings, SHAP analysis in this study confirmed lactate as a primary contributor to predicted AKI risk, with higher levels markedly increasing the model’s high-risk output probability. Nonetheless, beyond its pathogenic role, emerging evidence suggests potential reparative functions of lactate in spinal recovery, with studies linking it to lactylation-driven motor function restoration and neural regeneration [32,33]. Therefore, the dual nature of lactate underscores the need for contextual interpretation rather than reliance on a fixed threshold. In the acute management of TCTSCI, lactate should be measured at admission and reevaluated within the first 6–12 h, as a persistently elevated concentration or a lack of early decline may indicate renal hypoperfusion and call for timely optimization of hemodynamics, oxygen delivery, and early nephrology consultation [34]. In contrast, moderate and transient increases can reflect adaptive metabolic remodeling within the injured spinal cord that may contribute to recovery. Incorporating lactate trajectory monitoring into daily ICU evaluation offers a single, clinically accessible measure that functions both as an early warning signal of renal stress and as a potential indicator of neuro-metabolic repair, thereby supporting a balanced and actionable framework for individualized care in TCTSCI-associated AKI.

Elevated lactate in critically ill TCTSCI patients is often accompanied by metabolic acidosis, with serum bicarbonate reflecting the degree of acid–base imbalance [35]. In this study, patients with KDIGO stage 3 AKI exhibited significantly lower bicarbonate levels, and SHAP analysis revealed a negative association between bicarbonate and AKI risk, supporting its role as an early warning indicator. Prior research suggests that bicarbonate supplementation can attenuate acidosis-induced renal injury, particularly under impaired perfusion and sustained lactate production [36]. Accordingly, clinicians should closely monitor both lactate and bicarbonate levels during the early post-injury period in TCTSCI patients, as the coexistence of persistently elevated lactate and progressively declining bicarbonate may signal early renal hypoperfusion. Upon detection of such metabolic deterioration, prompt optimization of perfusion, reassessment of acid–base balance, and judicious consideration of bicarbonate therapy are warranted to mitigate progression to severe AKI [37].

Serum potassium was identified as a key driver of risk prediction in the MedFusion-GP-AKI model, with SHAP analysis demonstrating a clear positive association between hyperkalemia and the short-term occurrence of KDIGO stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients. Acute hyperkalemia in this population frequently results from trauma-induced rhabdomyolysis as well as abnormal activation of TWIK-related potassium channel 1 (TREK1) and ATP-sensitive potassium channels (KATP) within the spinal cord in response to local ischemia and reperfusion [38,39]. Studies by Hough and Fang have shown that these channels respond to metabolic and mechanical stress by promoting potassium efflux and neuronal membrane hyperpolarization, thereby reducing intracellular calcium influx and mitigating glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity, which aligns with the observed elevation in serum calcium among patients who developed KDIGO stage 3 AKI [38,40]. Clinically, hyperkalemia tends to occur more often in individuals with extensive or high-segment spinal injuries and is associated with poorer neurological outcomes [41]. Furthermore, the link between hyperkalemia and AKI has been well documented, as Chen et al. found that potassium concentrations ≥4.6 mmol/L significantly elevated the likelihood of AKI progression or mortality in patients with renal impairment [42]. Although traditionally viewed as a downstream consequence of renal impairment, growing evidence indicates that hyperkalemia may also act as an early precursor to AKI onset, with Lombardi and Ronco demonstrating that fluctuations in serum potassium can precede overt kidney injury and serve as subclinical markers of impending renal dysfunction [43,44]. These findings suggest that in TCTSCI patients, hyperkalemia may signal an early disruption of the neuro-renal axis rather than merely reflecting metabolic derangement [4]. Although activation of KATP and TREK1 potassium channels may transiently alleviate ischemia-induced neurotoxicity by promoting potassium efflux and reducing intracellular calcium overload, sustained extracellular potassium elevation can destabilize renal electrolyte balance and heighten susceptibility to AKI. Notably, Jonathan et al. underscored that dynamic surveillance of serum potassium, when integrated with assessments of neurological injury severity and perfusion status, may enable more accurate identification and stratification of individuals at high AKI risk [45]. Collectively, these findings identify hyperkalemia as a potential biomarker that not only links neural injury with renal vulnerability in TCTSCI but also signifies an integrated failure of neurogenic, vascular, and metabolic regulation that precedes overt kidney injury [46]. Recognizing this broader pathophysiological context transforms potassium monitoring from a routine laboratory measure into a dynamic instrument for assessing organ-system interactions in critical illness. Integrating potassium-trajectory analysis into multimodal ICU analytics, together with hemodynamic indices, injury level, and metabolic parameters, may enable precision risk stratification and guide physiologically informed interventions. Beyond monitoring, targeted modulation of potassium-channel or calcium-signaling pathways could further strengthen this systems-based approach by providing mechanistically grounded strategies with combined neuroprotective and renoprotective potential.

In the MedFusion-GP-AKI model, the spinal injury segment was incorporated as a core predictor not merely because it forms the anatomical basis of the American Spinal Injury Association (AISA) system, but because it serves as a fundamental determinant of systemic physiological disruption following trauma, as highlighted by Saadoun’s work, which reinforces lesion level as a key proxy for evaluating multiorgan vulnerability in acute spinal cord injury [47]. Unlike the ASIA score, which relies on neurological examination and may be infeasible in patients with impaired consciousness or deep sedation, the anatomical location of injury allows for rapid imaging-based evaluation and more directly reflects the extent to which essential autonomic functions, such as cardiovascular regulation and respiratory drive, are compromised [48]. Mounting evidence has linked higher segment spinal cord lesions to a markedly elevated risk of AKI, primarily due to the interruption of descending sympathetic pathways, which results in cardiac and vascular denervation, neurogenic shock characterized by concurrent bradycardia and vasodilation, and ultimately profound reductions in cardiac output and renal perfusion [2,29,49]. Even under conditions where blood pressure remains marginally preserved, Daniel et al. emphasized that persistent bradycardia can critically limit forward organ perfusion, thereby predisposing the renal parenchyma to ischemic injury and accelerating the onset of AKI [50]. Supporting this hemodynamic mechanism, SHAP analysis of the MedFusion-GP-AKI model revealed a consistently negative attribution weight for heart rate, suggesting that either preserved sympathetic tone or pharmacological chronotropic support may mitigate renal hypoperfusion and reduce AKI risk. Moreover, studies by Kuhlemeier and Doggart have shown that cervical and upper thoracic injuries can lead to persistent renal hemodynamic abnormalities extending into the chronic phase, with glomerular filtration rate declines manifesting even in patients whose early renal indices appeared normal, thereby indicating a progressive trajectory of renal impairment linked to injury height [51,52]. Consistent findings from Violeta et al. demonstrated that upper-level spinal lesions were associated with earlier and more severe reductions in renal function compared to lower-level injuries, further supporting an anatomically dependent gradient of AKI susceptibility [53]. Collectively, these findings highlight the need to redefine the role of injury level in acute spinal cord injury management [6]. Beyond its descriptive or diagnostic use, injury level should function as an early physiologic index of autonomic reserve and cardiovascular vulnerability, guiding both the intensity and timing of renal-protective interventions. For patients with cervical or upper thoracic injuries, early invasive hemodynamic monitoring, proactive maintenance of mean arterial pressure above neurogenic thresholds, and prompt correction of bradycardia are essential to sustain renal perfusion before overt injury develops. Incorporating injury level into standardized hemodynamic and renal-protection protocols could shift care from reactive stabilization to anticipatory prevention, ensuring that autonomic compromise is addressed before renal ischemia becomes irreversible. This systems-based approach reframes spinal injury not as an isolated neurological event but as a multi-organ crisis requiring level-specific strategies to preserve both neural and renal function.

Temperature emerged as a key causal factor for KDIGO stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients, with SHAP analysis highlighting its notable contribution to risk prediction within the MedFusion-GP-AKI framework. Prior evidence has suggested that temperature not only influences neurological recovery but also reflects early systemic perfusion status and renal vulnerability [48,54]. This study further supports such associations, demonstrating that patients who developed KDIGO stage 3 AKI during the acute phase exhibited significantly lower temperatures within 24 h of admission compared to those without, thereby indicating hypothermia as a potential early warning sign. Although fever is more commonly reported in TCTSCI patients, with an incidence ranging from 38.5% to 71.7%, its widespread occurrence and limited variability reduce its discriminative value for AKI risk [55,56]. In contrast, hypothermia, despite being less frequently documented, tends to occur in patients with high cervical or upper thoracic complete injuries, where disruption of thermoregulatory neural circuits compromises both heat production and dissipation, leaving patients reliant on passive environmental adaptation [57]. Studies by Colachis and Savage have shown that early hypothermia often signals severe spinal cord damage and is strongly associated with adverse short-term outcomes and multiorgan dysfunction [55,58]. Moreover, hypothermia itself contributes to impaired renal perfusion by inducing metabolic acidosis, myocardial depression, coagulopathy, and hemodynamic instability [59]. In TCTSCI patients, it frequently coincides with bradycardia and hypotension, forming a typical neurogenic shock pattern that severely compromises renal blood flow [60]. Animal models further support this mechanism, as sustained hypothermia in T4-level SCI exacerbates hemodynamic instability, whereas normothermia improves blood pressure and heart rate responses, underscoring the impact of thermal regulation on renal perfusion [61]. These findings highlight the importance of treating core temperature as an integral physiological signal rather than a peripheral vital sign in the early assessment of TCTSCI-associated AKI. Hypothermia should prompt clinicians to interpret renal risk within the broader context of autonomic failure and systemic hypoperfusion, guiding timely, physiology-based resuscitation to restore both thermal and circulatory homeostasis. Equally important, therapeutic hypothermia should not be applied empirically without continuous hemodynamic monitoring, as indiscriminate cooling may mask evolving perfusion deficits and heighten the risk of kidney injury. Incorporating core temperature into early risk-assessment protocols can facilitate earlier recognition of circulatory instability and more targeted interventions to maintain renal perfusion in acute spinal trauma.

MAP, highlighted by the MedFusion-GP-AKI model as a major predictor, plays a central role in supporting hemodynamic balance and systemic perfusion in critically ill TCTSCI patients. Beyond its contribution to secondary spinal cord ischemia, a reduction in MAP directly impairs renal perfusion once it falls below the autoregulatory threshold, leading to a rapid decline in renal blood flow [62]. In the absence of effective compensatory mechanisms, reduced renal perfusion renders tubular epithelial cells highly vulnerable to ischemia–reperfusion damage and subsequent acute tubular necrosis [63], a process that during the early phase of TCTSCI is further intensified by inflammatory activation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, collectively aggravating renal impairment and accelerating progression toward severe AKI [64]. Although the initial rationale for maintaining elevated MAP centered on optimizing spinal cord perfusion, current guidelines have progressively expanded its recommended indications toward broader multi-organ protection, with particular emphasis on preserving renal perfusion and function [65]. The MedFusion-GP-AKI model supports this view, with SHAP analysis showing that MAP provided greater explanatory power than traditional predictors and indicating that early MAP decline in TCTSCI primarily reflects sympathetic failure and loss of vascular tone rather than true volume depletion. This pathophysiologic pattern explains why hypotension in these patients often fails to respond to fluid resuscitation alone and instead requires vasopressor therapy to reestablish perfusion pressure [66]. Previous studies have shown that nearly 80% of patients with cervical spinal cord injury require vasopressors to maintain guideline-recommended MAP values, frequently for several days, suggesting a substantial dependence on pharmacologic support for vascular tone [67]. In this study, vasopressor use was significantly more common in the non-AKI group, implying a protective association with timely hemodynamic intervention. Consistent with this observation, previous studies have reported that vasopressors, when appropriately titrated to maintain MAP within recommended thresholds, do not increase AKI risk and may help preserve renal perfusion by correcting neurogenic hypotension [68,69], whereas strategies that tolerate lower pressures to minimize vasopressor exposure have been associated with higher rates of postoperative AKI [66]. Collectively, these findings indicate that in TCTSCI, mean arterial pressure should be viewed not merely as a perfusion target for the injured spinal cord but as a dynamic indicator of renal function adequacy. Even a modest decline in MAP within the conventionally acceptable range may reflect early renal hypoperfusion, warranting immediate reassessment of vascular tone, circulating volume, and overall hemodynamic stability. Timely initiation and precise titration of vasopressor therapy, rather than delayed or excessive fluid resuscitation, appear to confer superior protection against ischemic acute kidney injury in this population, emphasizing the importance of tailoring hemodynamic management to the integrated requirements of both neurological and renal systems.

In the context of TCTSCI, a complex interplay between preexisting frailty and trauma-induced systemic derangements markedly amplifies renal vulnerability from the earliest stages of injury, whereby a higher CCI, indicative of a substantial chronic disease burden, reflects diminished renal reserve and reduced physiological capacity to withstand the profound hemodynamic fluctuations and inflammatory surges triggered by TCTSCI, thereby predisposing patients to acute kidney injury [70–72]. Concomitantly, a lower GCS score at admission, often associated with severe trauma and concomitant brain injury, signals exaggerated neurohumoral stress response characterized by massive catecholamine release and immune dysregulation, which collectively impair renal perfusion and aggravate tubular damage [73,74]. Furthermore, traumatic spinal cord injury can trigger a systemic inflammatory cascade, initially manifested as peripheral leukocytosis that serves as a clinical indicator of robust cytokine release, which in turn propagates renal damage by inducing widespread microvascular dysfunction and amplifying oxidative stress, thereby accelerating the onset and severity of AKI [75,76]. From a clinical perspective, early identification of systemic stress indicators, particularly elevated CCI, reduced GCS, and marked WBC, should prompt heightened vigilance for increased renal susceptibility even in the absence of overt creatinine elevation. Integrating these routinely available indices into the initial triage process and subsequent hemodynamic management may enable more proactive risk stratification, facilitate intensified renal surveillance, and support timely therapeutic interventions aimed at preventing progression to severe acute kidney injury.

This study proposes a novel deep learning framework, MedFusion-GP-AKI, to predict stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients. While the model exhibits favorable predictive accuracy and satisfactory generalizability across internal and external cohorts, several limitations should be acknowledged and contextualized. First, the low event rate of KDIGO stage 3 AKI limited the number of positive cases available for model training. To address this challenge, the study applied a SMOTified-GAN approach to generate synthetic minority-class samples based on the observed data distribution, effectively enhancing class balance and mitigating overfitting risk. Additionally, a generative adversarial imputation network was used to recover missing values in key variables, thereby preserving sample integrity and reducing selection bias. Despite these measures, the reliance on synthetic data may still introduce unobserved biases that warrant further evaluation. Second, although the study employed multiple feature selection algorithms, including variational bottleneck extraction, causal graph modeling, and counterfactual contribution analysis, to reduce noise and improve interpretability, the retrospective design inherently limits the ability to control for latent confounders, and some degree of residual overfitting or non-causal associations cannot be entirely excluded. Third, although the model was trained and internally validated using large-scale public datasets from the United States and externally tested on multicenter cohorts from four institutions in China, the absence of data from other geographic regions precludes a complete determination of its generalizability across diverse global healthcare systems. Further cross-national validation is needed to more comprehensively assess its applicability in heterogeneous clinical contexts. Fourth, this study focused exclusively on early AKI prediction within seven days after injury without incorporating time-series data or long-term renal outcomes such as dialysis dependence or hospital mortality, which may limit the model’s utility for extended prognostic assessment. Fifth, although the model integrated a broad range of routinely collected variables spanning neurological status, vital signs, and laboratory indicators, several potentially important parameters, such as fluid balance and inflammatory biomarkers, were unavailable or incompletely recorded in the American and Chinese datasets, which may have restricted the comprehensiveness of risk modeling. Finally, the MedFusion-GP-AKI model should be regarded as a retrospective proof-of-concept framework intended to complement, rather than supplant, clinical judgment. By providing early risk alerts, it enables the timely recognition of patients susceptible to severe AKI and offers decision support to guide, rather than dictate, therapeutic management. Nevertheless, as a preliminary framework developed under retrospective conditions, MedFusion-GP-AKI warrants cautious interpretation, with its generalizability and real-world impact remaining to be verified through prospective evaluation and longitudinal observation.

To address these limitations and advance MedFusion-GP-AKI toward clinical translation, future research should pursue an integrated trajectory that unites prospective validation, adaptive intelligence, cross-institutional scalability, and transparent governance within a single translational continuum. The highest priority is to conduct a rigorously designed, pre-registered multicenter prospective evaluation that continuously monitors model drift, determines appropriate update intervals, and defines real-world safety thresholds across diverse intensive care and spinal cord injury populations, thereby ensuring stable performance under heterogeneous clinical conditions. Building upon such empirical validation, MedFusion-GP-AKI should evolve from a static prediction framework into a continuously learning clinical intelligence system capable of assimilating dynamic physiologic signals, bedside imaging, and laboratory time-series data including evolving MAP, lactate trajectories, and temperature variations, so that the model can extend its predictive scope beyond the current short-term horizon and adapt to the temporal complexity of critical illness. This continuous integration would establish the conceptual foundation for developing ICU digital twin architectures, in which the fusion-level ensemble serves as a causality-informed predictive core that recalibrates risk trajectories in near real time through the assimilation of streaming clinical data. Within such virtual patient representations, it would be possible to simulate alternative hemodynamic or therapeutic strategies and to generate counterfactual guidance, for instance, estimating the reduction in kidney injury risk that might result from earlier vasopressor titration or targeted lactate clearance, thus enabling proactive and individualized intervention design. To realize cross-institutional scalability while preserving patient privacy, future studies should explore federated and privacy-preserving learning frameworks that allow decentralized model aggregation and site-specific recalibration, ensuring probability fidelity across institutions without centralizing sensitive data. In parallel, technical innovation must be coupled with a robust governance infrastructure that aligns with TRIPOD-AI and PROBAST-AI reporting standards, incorporates interpretability tools such as model cards, and establishes transparent documentation pipelines that support accountability, regulatory readiness, and ethical oversight. Ultimately, embedding MedFusion-GP-AKI within interoperable electronic health record environments as a clinician-facing, continuously adaptive decision-support system would represent a critical step toward the creation of a closed-loop, interpretable, and ethically governed AI ecosystem for precision kidney care in critically ill TCTSCI patients, consistent with the guiding principles articulated in the American Society of Nephrology Artificial Intelligence Statement [77].

This study presents MedFusion-GP-AKI, an ensemble deep learning model that harnesses routinely collected ICU data from the first 24 h of admission to predict the seven-day risk of KDIGO stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients with high accuracy and consistency across internal and external cohorts. By modeling the complex, nonlinear interplay among hemodynamic parameters, metabolic biomarkers, clinical scoring systems, and injury-specific features, MedFusion-GP-AKI enables early identification of high-risk individuals, thereby informing targeted hemodynamic optimization, avoidance of nephrotoxins, and timely consideration of renal support modalities. Rather than replacing clinical judgment, the model is intended to augment decision-making under conditions of prognostic uncertainty, particularly in the management of critically ill spinal cord injury patients with high AKI risk. Future prospective multicenter studies are needed to evaluate its implementation in real-time clinical workflows and its potential to improve renal outcomes, resource allocation, and long-term prognosis in this vulnerable population.

sections.title: Ethical approval and consent to participate

paragraphs.en: This study was conducted using data from the MIMIC-IV (version 3.1) and eICU Collaborative Research Database (version 2.0), both of which are publicly available, fully de-identified critical care datasets. Access was granted upon completion of the required training and credentialing through PhysioNet (Certificated ID: 57264471). The use of these databases was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, with a waiver of informed consent due to the retrospective nature of the study and the use of de-identified data. In addition, the use of clinical data from the First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University, People’s Hospital of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Chongqing University Three Gorges Hospital, Jingzhou First People’s Hospital was approved by the each institutional ethics committee (Approval No. K202404-45, KY2024052264, SXYYWD2022-058, YJ202376). Informed consent was waived as all patients’ legal representatives had signed electronic consent forms upon ICU admission, authorizing the use of anonymized data for scientific research.

The MIMIC-IV (version 3.1) and eICU Collaborative Research Database (version 2.0) are publicly available from the PhysioNet repository (https://physionet.org/) following credentialed access approval. Clinical data collected from the First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University, the People’s Hospital of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Chongqing University Three Gorges Hospital, as well as Jingzhou First People’s Hospital, which were fully de-identified prior to analysis, have been deposited as an anonymized external validation dataset in Zenodo and are publicly available at DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17385515. Model-related information can be found on GitHub (https://github.com/Numwyx/MedFusion-GP-AKI).

Develops MedFusion-GP-AKI, a fusion-level ensemble framework integrating categorical-embedding attention, multimodal gated fusion, residual Transformer encoders, differentiable deep forests, and a deep-kernel Gaussian-process head for uncertainty-aware prediction, thereby extending beyond conventional meta-stacking approaches.

Demonstrates real-world generalizability through internal validation on combined MIMIC-IV/eICU datasets and external validation across four tertiary critical-care centers in China, showing consistent discrimination, calibration, and net clinical benefit across healthcare systems.

Translates the model into a fully deployable, web-based prediction calculator that provides early, individualized risk estimation using standard ICU variables within the first 24 hours of admission, assisting clinicians in assessing patient risk and implementing targeted interventions.

Establishes a pathophysiologic linkage between spinal cord injury–related neurogenic shock and acute kidney injury by integrating metabolic indicators such as serum lactate, hemodynamic measures including mean arterial pressure and heart rate, and neurological characteristics such as Glasgow Coma Scale scores and injury features into a unified causal framework, thereby connecting autonomic dysregulation with renal vulnerability.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: Study workflow for the development, validation, and interpretation of the MedFusion-GP-AKI model for predicting KIDGO stage 3 AKI in critically ill TCTSCI patients.From 1,046 patients identified in the MIMIC-IV and eICU databases, 996 were retained after excluding those younger than 18 years or with excessive missing data. These patients were categorized into non-AKI (n = 406), stage 1 (n = 152), stage 2 (n = 298), and stage 3 (n = 140), yielding 856 non–stage 3 and 140 stage 3 AKI cases. The pre-SMOTE dataset was divided into a training set of 697 patients (98 stage 3 AKI and 599 non–stage 3 AKI) and a test set of 299 patients (42 stage 3 AKI and 257 non–stage 3 AKI) for baseline evaluation. To address class imbalance, a SMOTified-GAN was then applied to generate synthetic stage 3 AKI samples, resulting in a balanced dataset of 1,712 patients. This balanced dataset was further divided into a training cohort of 1,198 patients (633 stage 3 AKI and 565 non–stage 3 AKI) and a test cohort of 514 patients (288 stage 3 AKI and 286 non–stage 3 AKI) for model development and validation. Subsequently, feature selection integrating VIB, ACAE, and NOTEARS was performed to identify clinically relevant predictors. Fifteen machine learning models, including XGBoost, TabNet, SVM, RF, SAINT, NODE, LR, LightGBM, KNN, GBM, DKL, FT Transformer, CatBoost, AdaBoost, and MLP, were then trained and evaluated on both the original imbalanced dataset and the SMOTified-GAN balanced dataset through ROC, calibration, precision–recall, decision-curve, and gain-curve analyses, together with accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1 metrics. Models with relatively superior performance were subsequently integrated into the MedFusion-GP-AKI ensemble, which was validated across both the original and balanced datasets in their respective training and validation cohorts, and further evaluated in an external cohort of 188 critically ill TCTSCI patients from four tertiary hospitals in China (67 stage 3 AKI and 121 non–stage 3 AKI). Model interpretation and clinical deployment were supported by SHAP analysis and a web-based risk calculator.

figures.caption: Sixty-day Kaplan–Meier survival curves stratified by KDIGO AKI severity in critically ill TCTSCI patients.Kaplan–Meier survival analysis demonstrating the cumulative probability of survival within 60 days among critically ill TCTSCI patients stratified by KDIGO AKI severity. Patients without AKI exhibited the highest survival probability throughout the observation period, followed by those with stage 1 and stage 2 AKI, whereas patients with stage 3 AKI showed a markedly reduced survival probability with an early and steep decline within the first two weeks that continued to diverge over time. The overall differences across groups were statistically significant (log-rank test, p < 0.0001).
